Neonatal Thorny skate, Amblyraja radiata, emerge from their egg cases at a total length of approximately 10 centimeters [Lb = approximately 10 centimeters], though field-collected neonates typically display a range in total length from 8 to 12 cm [Lb = 8 to 12 cm]. This modest size at birth places the species among the smaller-skated young in the North Atlantic, where the yolk-dependent embryos of this oviparous elasmobranch develop within tough, dark-colored egg capsules deposited on the seabed. The incubation period, which is heavily influenced by ambient water temperature, has been documented to last about 335.5 days [ab = about 335.5 days] when embryos are maintained at a constant temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This exceptionally long developmental phase reflects the cold, deep-water environment the species inhabits, where metabolic rates are inherently low and embryonic growth proceeds at a deliberate pace. The protracted incubation is consistent with the general pattern observed among boreal and Arctic skates, contrasting sharply with the shorter embryonic periods of temperate congeners. Newly hatched individuals are fully formed miniatures of the adults, bearing the characteristic thorn-like dermal denticles along their tails and disc margins, and they begin foraging on small benthic invertebrates almost immediately after yolk-sac resorption.

As the Thorny skate progresses through its juvenile and sub-adult stages, it eventually attains sexual maturation when its total length reaches approximately 87.5 cm [Lp = approximately 87.5 cm]. This length at puberty is a critical life-history parameter, as it marks the point at which individuals shift energetic investment from somatic growth toward reproductive activities. The species exhibits clear sexual dimorphism in size, with females typically growing larger than males, a pattern commonly observed in elasmobranchs where larger body size confers increased fecundity. Once puberty is achieved, the maximum total length recorded for this species in the Northwestern Atlantic is 105 cm [Li = 105 cm], a value obtained from a large female captured during a groundfish survey off the Grand Banks. Adult body mass correspondingly reaches an ultimate wet weight of 11,400 grams [Wwi = 11,400 grams], a substantial figure that underscores the robust, heavy-bodied build of the species relative to other members of its genus. Field studies indicate that growth slows markedly after the attainment of sexual maturity, with negligible increases in length observed beyond the midpoint of the lifespan.

Reproductive output in Amblyraja radiata is modest compared to many teleost fishes, reflecting the energetic constraints of producing large, well-yolked eggs in cold waters. Females deposit their eggs in pairs over an extended breeding season, with the maximum observed egg production rate reaching 22 eggs per year [Ri = 22 eggs per year] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This translates to a fecundity of approximately 10 to 45 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 10 to 45 eggs per year] depending on female size and local food availability. Each egg case contains a single developing embryo and is provisioned with a substantial yolk supply that sustains the embryo through its lengthy incubation. The reproductive strategy of producing few, large, heavily provisioned offspring is a classic K-selected life-history pattern common among deepwater elasmobranchs, prioritizing offspring survival in a stable but resource-poor environment. Females are believed to have a biennial or triennial reproductive cycle in some populations, though continuous annual breeding has been documented in regions with higher prey abundance.

Lifespan data for the Thorny skate, derived from mark-recapture studies and vertebral band-pair analysis, indicate that individuals can live for approximately 16 years [am = approximately 16 years] at a temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C]. This maximum longevity is relatively short compared to some other skates, such as the long-lived Bathyraja species of the deep North Pacific, but is consistent with the moderate lifespan expectations of a boreal elasmobranch with a relatively fast growth rate during its early years. The age at which natural mortality begins to increase due to senescence has not been precisely determined, but field observations suggest that post-reproductive mortality occurs primarily in the later years of life. The combination of a moderate lifespan, delayed maturity, and low fecundity renders Amblyraja radiata particularly vulnerable to overexploitation. Population modeling has shown that fishing mortality rates exceeding a few percent per year can rapidly lead to stock declines, as the species cannot compensate through increased recruitment. Consequently, conservation measures such as size limits and seasonal closures have been implemented in parts of its range to protect mature adults.

Comparative studies of life-history traits across the Rajidae family highlight the intermediate position of Amblyraja radiata. The length at first reproduction, at around 87.5 cm [Lp = around 87.5 cm] total length, corresponds to roughly 83 percent of the maximum attainable size of 105 cm [Li = 105 cm], a proportion typical of many skate species that mature relatively late relative to their asymptotic length. In contrast, the maximum reproductive rate of 10 to 45 eggs per year [Ri = 10 to 45 eggs per year] is low even by elasmobranch standards, placing the Thorny skate among the less fecund members of its guild. Weighing approximately 11.4 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 11.4 kilograms] as a fully grown adult, this species exhibits a mass-to-length ratio that is typical of robust rajids, reflecting its adaptation to cold, deep-water habitats where heavy body armor of dermal denticles contributes to overall weight. Ecologically, the species occupies a broad depth range from the intertidal to over 1000 meters, but shows a preference for soft sediment habitats where it preys on crustaceans, polychaetes, and small fish. This dietary flexibility likely buffers it against fluctuations in individual prey populations, though the energetic costs of foraging at depth impose constraints on growth and reproductive output.
